          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.",

          "quote": "An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor

          "quote": "Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**

path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.",

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is a rational, and that is not a matter of taste.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies $a^{r}$ for a nonnegative base and a **rational**
exponent only; real exponents do not exist at this point in the reading order,
and [[rem-real-exponents-deferred]] records exactly why. This is also why the
published Minkowski inequality [[thm-minkowski-finite]], which is what makes the
triangle inequality work below, is itself stated for rational $p \ge 1$. **No
statement on this page is written for $p$ ranging over a real interval.**

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled

Then $h(v,w)=\eta(h(v),h(w))$ for the orthogonal projection $h(v):=v+\eta(n,v)n$ of [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] clause (c). **(b) Acceleration.** The **acceleration** of the congruence is $a:=\nabla_nn$. Then $\eta(n,a)=0$ pointwise, because $2\eta(n,\nabla_nn)=n\bigl(\eta(n,n)\bigr)=0$; consequently $a(p)$ is spacelike or zero by the causal classification ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). In the model's physical interpretation the four-acceleration of the congruence observers is $c^2a$ and its magnitude is $c^2\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}$; the numerical units belong to the model's SI conventions and are not part of the affine geometry ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]).

$$\nabla_an_b=-n_aa_b+\theta_{ab}+\omega_{ab},$$

with $\theta$ symmetric, $\omega$ antisymmetric, both horizontal ($\theta_{ab}n^b=\omega_{ab}n^b=n^a\theta_{ab}=n^a\omega_{ab}=0$), and this decomposition is unique with these properties. The tensor $\theta$ is the **expansion (and shear) tensor**, $\theta:=h^{ab}\theta_{ab}$ is the **expansion scalar**, its trace-free part is the **shear**, and $\omega$ is the **vorticity 2-tensor**.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting

3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$

chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when

  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number

          "quote": "Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space

space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted

$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows

for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

          "quote": "Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.",

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**(a) Vector fields.** For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $\Omega$ define the **covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction $X$** at $p\in\Omega$ by

$$\bigl(\nabla_XY\bigr)(p):=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}Y\bigl(p+tX(p)\bigr),$$

the derivative of the $V$-valued composite $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$, which is defined for $t$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ because $\Omega$ is open ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-derivative]]). In the inertial chart $x$ of any inertial frame one has $(\nabla_XY)^a=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$; the value does not depend on the inertial chart: for another inertial chart $x'=\Lambda x+b$ one has $\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b_{\ a}\,\partial_b$ and $Y'^a=\Lambda^a_{\ b}Y^b$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]], [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and $\Lambda$ is constant, so $(\Lambda^{-1})^a_{\ c}\,X'^b\,\partial'_bY'^c=X^b\,\partial_bY^a$. The field $\nabla_XY$ is again a smooth vector field on $\Omega$.

**(b) Covector and general tensor fields.** For a smooth covector field $\alpha$ set $(\nabla_X\alpha)(Y):=X(\alpha(Y))-\alpha(\nabla_XY)$ for every smooth vector field $Y$, and for a type $(r,s)$ tensor field $T$ define $\nabla_XT$ by the derivation rule on the evaluation of $T$: for $T:(V^*)^r\times V^s\to\mathbb R$,

$$(\nabla_XT)(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)=X\bigl[T(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)\bigr]-\sum_{i=1}^rT(\alpha_1,\dots,\nabla_X\alpha_i,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,Y_s)-\sum_{j=1}^sT(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r;Y_1,\dots,\nabla_XY_j,\dots,Y_s),$$

where the vector and covector arguments are smooth fields on $\Omega$. In inertial coordinates every component of $\nabla_XT$ is $X^b\,\partial_b$ applied to that component, with no connection coefficients.

**(c) Properties.** The operator $\nabla$ is $\mathbb R$-bilinear, is $C^\infty(\Omega)$-linear in $X$, and satisfies the Leibniz rules $\nabla_X(fY)=X(f)Y+f\nabla_XY$ and the analogous rules for tensor fields; it is metric compatible, $\nabla\eta=0$, because $\partial_a\eta_{bc}=0$ in every inertial chart; it is torsion-free, $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX=[X,Y]$, by the coordinate formula for the Lie bracket ([[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], [[prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket]]); and it has zero curvature, $\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z=0$, by equality of mixed partial derivatives of the components ([[thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem]]).

**(d) Fields along a curve.** If $\gamma:I\to A$ is a $C^1$ curve and $W:I\to V$ is a $C^1$ field along it ([[def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve]]), the **covariant derivative of $W$ along $\gamma$** is the ordinary $V$-valued derivative $DW/ds:=W'$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), because the canonical identification $T_pA=V$ is independent of $p$; consequently parallel transport along any curve is the identity and a field is parallel exactly when it is constant. No $C^1$ closure of this bracket and no second covariant derivative of arbitrary $C^1$ data are asserted. For $C^2$ vector fields the second derivatives needed for the zero-curvature identity of (c) exist, and that identity follows by equality of the continuous mixed second partials.    form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.

   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all

   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.

3-dimensional linear subspace of $V$, the restriction of $\eta$ to $n^{\perp}$

linear, idempotent with $h \circ h = h$, has image $n^{\perp}$ and kernel
$\operatorname{span}(n)$, satisfies $h(n) = 0$ and $\eta(n,h(v)) = 0$ for all
$v \in V$, and every $v \in V$ has the unique decomposition
$v = -\eta(n,v)\,n + h(v)$. Moreover $|w| := \sqrt{\eta(w,w)}$ defines a norm
on $n^{\perp}$.

timelike vectors, put $\gamma := -\eta(n,u)$ and $w := c\,h(u)/\gamma$. Then
$\gamma \ge 1$, $w$ lies in $n^{\perp}$,
$u = \gamma\,(n + w/c)$, $|w|^{2} = c^{2}(1-\gamma^{-2}) < c^{2}$,

to the observer $n$, and $\gamma$ is its Lorentz factor.

$y$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline whose inertial coordinates are
$t \mapsto (ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w(t) := r'(t)$ in

$a(t) := w'(t)$. Then $|w(t)| < c$, the four-velocity is
$U = \gamma_w\,(c,w)$ with $\gamma_w := (1-|w|^{2}/c^{2})^{-1/2}$, and the

$\gamma = \gamma_w$ and $w_{\mathrm{rel}} = w$.

a fixed positive constant $c$; it asserts no clock reading and identifies no

          "quote": "Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and

$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

          "quote": "Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.",

          "quote": "Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

where $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, with charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]). Write the transition as

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr),\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr),\qquad x'^2=x^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with $x$-separation $L_0$ the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

**(iv) Velocity transformation.** Let $y:J\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline which in the chart $x$ is $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with coordinate velocity $w(t):=r'(t)\in\mathbb R^3$, $|w(t)|<c$, and $\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$.           "source_section": "Definition",
          "quote": "Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.",

$$\bigl(\nabla_XY\bigr)(p):=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}Y\bigl(p+tX(p)\bigr),$$

the derivative of the $V$-valued composite $t\mapsto Y(p+tX(p))$, which is defined for $t$ in a neighbourhood of $0$ because $\Omega$ is open ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-derivative]]).
